disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent, excessive preoccupation with perceived defects in physical appearance that are minimal or not observable to others, leading to marked distress or impairment. Individuals commonly engage in repetitive behaviors (such as mirror checking, grooming, skin picking, or seeking reassurance) or mental acts (such as comparing themselves to others) in response to these concerns. Onset is often in adolescence or early adulthood, with a typically chronic course that can wax and wane in intensity and is frequently exacerbated by social evaluation, transitions, or appearance-focused environments. BDD is distinguished from normal appearance concerns and eating disorders by the disproportionate distress, time consumption, and functional impairment related to specific perceived flaws, and from psychotic disorders by generally intact reality testing outside of appearance beliefs, though insight can range from good to delusional.

narrative.stressor: Over the past few years, as Edilma advanced in her role and her company shifted more support interactions to video-based platforms and client-facing webinars, she became increasingly focused on how she looked on camera during calls and recorded trainings. A couple of offhand comments from coworkers about looking "tired" on screen and a particularly unflattering still frame from a recorded webinar stuck with her, and she began rearranging her schedule and declining opportunities that involved being on video or photographed at community tech events. Her active social life—dancing, soccer, festivals—started to feel more like a minefield of situations where she might be tagged in photos or appear on social media, and she found herself hesitating to join outings she once organized. When she missed a chance at a promotion because she declined to lead a highly visible training series, and her manager gently raised concerns about her sudden avoidance of public-facing tasks, she finally agreed to see a psychiatrist at the urging of a close friend from her Latino community group.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t stop fixating on how awful I look on camera and in photos, and it’s starting to affect my work and social life.”

narrative.stressor: Eric traces the intensification of his appearance concerns to the period surrounding his divorce three years ago, when his ex-wife began dating a younger, very fit partner and friends made casual jokes about him "going gray overnight." As a middle-aged advisor working with affluent clients and mingling at gallery openings, he became acutely aware of being photographed for firm marketing materials and social events, interpreting any glance or pause as a silent judgment about how he looked compared with his clients and peers. Over time, he started turning down speaking engagements, avoiding social gatherings where photos might be taken, and scheduling client meetings only by phone, which began to hurt his book of business and drew criticism from his firm’s partners. When his teenage daughter asked why he never wanted to be in family pictures anymore and his supervisor warned him that his withdrawal was jeopardizing his position, he finally sought psychiatric help, describing that his life had become dominated by worry about a specific aspect of his appearance.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I spend so much time checking and trying to fix this one thing about how I look that it’s taking over my day and costing me work.”

narrative.stressor: For Sunita, her long-standing sensitivity about how she looks intensified as she entered her early fifties, coinciding with perimenopausal changes, her children leaving for college, and a shift in her firm toward younger hires who were frequently featured in marketing materials. Preparing to attend industry conferences and temple functions where she once felt at ease, she began dreading the prospect of being seen in bright lighting, photographed, or running into old acquaintances, and she started over-planning outfits and schedules to minimize such situations. Her husband and close friends noticed she was declining invitations to cultural festivals she used to help organize and was increasingly reluctant to present her own design work at client meetings, delegating public-facing roles to junior staff despite her seniority. When she skipped a long-planned family trip because she felt she "couldn’t bear" being in vacation photos and her avoidance began to strain both work responsibilities and family relationships, her primary care physician, seeing how much this preoccupation was affecting her functioning, referred her for psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I’m constantly worried about how I look as I’m getting older, and it’s making me avoid family events and work presentations.”
